## Summary

The reference case. A lost war, reparations the state would not tax for, and a central bank that bought the government's bills without limit took the mark from 4.2 per dollar in 1914 to 4.2 trillion in November 1923. Prices peaked in **October 1923, rising 29,500% in a single month and doubling every 3.70 days** (H&K). It ended within weeks once the Reichsbank was barred from financing the state and a new unit, the Rentenmark, replaced the paper mark.

## Causes

- **War finance.** Germany paid for 1914–18 with borrowing and money, not taxes, expecting the
  loser to pay. The mark had already lost most of its value by 1919 (48/USD).
- **Reparations.** The London Schedule (May 1921) set 132 billion gold marks. Payments in gold or
  foreign currency meant selling marks for dollars, which pushed the mark down.
- **The central bank as the Treasury's buyer.** The Reichsbank discounted government Treasury bills
  without limit; each bill became new paper marks. This is the mechanism, and stopping it is what
  ended the inflation (see *The end*).
- **The Ruhr.** In January 1923 French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr after a default on
  deliveries. The government backed passive resistance by paying idle workers — with printed money
  — while losing the output of its industrial heart. 1923 is when inflation became hyperinflation.

## Timeline

- **1914–1918** — war financed by debt; 4.2 → 7.9 marks per dollar.
- **May 1921** — London Schedule: 132 bn gold marks of reparations.
- **mid-1922** — 320 marks per dollar; **August 1922** inflation crosses 50%/month (H&K start).
- **December 1922** — 7,400 marks per dollar.
- **January 1923** — occupation of the Ruhr; passive resistance financed by the press.
- **August 1923** — Helfferich proposes a rye-backed "Roggenmark", the idea behind the Rentenmark.
- **October 1923** — peak: +29,500% in the month, prices doubling every 3.70 days (H&K).
- **12 November 1923** — Hjalmar Schacht becomes currency commissioner; the Reichsbank may no
  longer discount Treasury bills.
- **16 November 1923** — the Rentenmark is introduced; twelve zeros cut.
- **20 November 1923** — Reichsbank president Rudolf Havenstein dies; the dollar is at ≈ 4.2 trillion.
- **1924** — Dawes Plan restarts reparations on a payable schedule; **30 August 1924** monetary law:
  1 trillion paper marks = 1 Reichsmark (= 1 Rentenmark).

## Life during it

- Workers were paid daily, then twice a day, and spent the money within hours.
- A Berlin loaf went from about 160 marks at the end of 1922 to 200 billion marks in late 1923.
- Savings, pensions, life insurance and war bonds — the middle class's wealth — were wiped out;
  debtors (including the state and anyone with a mortgage) were freed of their debts.
- Towns and firms printed their own emergency money (*Notgeld*) when the Reichsbank could not keep up.

## The end

Three things at once, in November 1923: (1) the Reichsbank stopped discounting Treasury bills — the ban, which is the reform; (2) a new unit, the **Rentenmark**, nominally backed by a mortgage on German land and industry, issued in a strictly limited amount; (3) budget cuts. The price level held from late November. The Dawes Plan (1924) made reparations payable and brought foreign loans; the **Reichsmark** replaced both marks from August 1924.

## Lessons

- The press is the mechanism; the deficit financed by the central bank is the cause.
- The Rentenmark's "backing" could never be redeemed — its strength was the **limit** on its
  quantity and the ban on financing the state, i.e. credibility, not collateral.
- The fear of 1923 shaped German monetary policy for a century (Bundesbank, then the ECB mandate).
